title: When did we start living longer?
hook: World life expectancy crept up 3 years in the 1800s. What did the next century add?

knows: that people live longer now than in the past
that life expectancy at birth is an average over everyone born (history:life-expectancy-vs-lifespan)
doesNotKnow: that almost all the gain came in one century: about 3 years in the 1800s against about 35 in the 1900s

misconception: Life expectancy has risen gradually for centuries.
objective: The learner can say that in Gapminder's world series life expectancy rose about 2.8 years over the 1800s (30.6 to 33.5) and about 34.7 years over the 1900s (to 68.2), about 12 times as much, and that the series is one source's estimate shown at one point every 25 years.

claims.text: Over the 1800s world life expectancy rose 2.9 years (30.6 to 33.5, as shown); over the 1900s it rose 34.7 years, about 12 times as much; from 2000 to 2023, a span of 23 years, it rose 5.8 years (readouts '+2.9 yrs', '+34.7 yrs'; 'Years gained in each span' bars '+2.9', '+34.7', '+5.8', named '1800 to 1900 (100 years)', '1900 to 2000 (100 years)', '2000 to 2023 (23 years)'; reveal; hook 'crept up 3 years in the 1800s').
claims.source: Gains are differences of the one-decimal values shown (Demo.tsx gain = shown(b) - shown(a)), so a learner's subtraction on screen comes out: 33.5 - 30.6 = 2.9; 68.2 - 33.5 = 34.7; 74.0 - 68.2 = 5.8; 34.7 / 2.9 = 11.97, rounded to 12. Unrounded, from history-data.mjs: gmlex, gapminder-lex-global.csv, world, lex (re-derived in node 2026-10-15): 33.48469 - 30.64173 = 2.84; 68.20445 - 33.48469 = 34.72; 74.04122 - 68.20445 = 5.84; 34.72 / 2.84 = 12.2, also 12. So the shown 2.9 is the rounded endpoints' difference; the unrounded gain is 2.84. history-cycle2-check.mjs section 14 ('two centuries', '2000 to 2023') quotes 2.8. The hook rounds to 3.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): +2.843, +34.720, ratio 12.21 (12), 2000-2023 +5.837 (5.8); hook rounds 2.8 to 3. | v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-15, W-990, learner r1 finding 2): was '+2.8 (30.6 → 33.5)', which fails a beginner's subtraction; now the gain of the shown values, 2.9; the bars view is labelled as spans with their lengths, not 'per century' (finding 1). Reset to unverified for a fact-checker who is not the builder.

recall.question: A country's life expectancy rose 3 years in one century and 30 in the next. What share of the two centuries' gain came in the second?
recall.why: 30 of the 33 years gained is about 90%: when one century's gain is ten times the other's, nearly all of the rise sits in the later century, as with the world's 2.8 years in the 1800s against 34.7 in the 1900s.
